data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's position is unstable because 'severity' of tests cannot be defined without inductive background knowledge, making the entire edifice of corroboration dependent on the very thing it rejects.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'severity' can be defined purely logically or syntactically without reference to empirical probabilities.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If background knowledge is treated as conjectural and subject to falsification, breaking the inductive chain.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'background dependence'. A test is only 'severe' if we have good reason to believe the outcome is unlikely given current knowledge. Assessing this 'unlikelihood' requires inductive confidence in our background theories. Therefore, corroboration is parasitic on induction. The preference for corroborated theories is thus doubly inductive: once in defining the test, and again in projecting the result. This costs Popper the purity of his demarcation criterion.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
